title: Reasons for the commandments
hookLine: Maimonides looks for reasons behind the laws; others say some have none we can know

cards: What is this for? Put that question to the commandments, and you meet two very different answers inside Judaism. One says: ask.
There is wisdom here, and you can find it. The other says: some of these you keep because God commanded them, and the reason may stay hidden. Both answers come from teachers of the same Torah.
Maimonides plants himself firmly on one side.

teach.b: Ta'amei hamitzvot: the reasons for the commandments. Ta'am is the word for taste, and also for reason, the flavor of sense inside a law. First, Maimonides' claim.
In the third part of the Guide he says every commandment has a reason and serves a purpose: to teach a true idea, to correct a habit, to build a fair society.
Some people dislike giving reasons, he notices, as if a law with no explanation were more divine.
He thinks they have it backward, and quotes Deuteronomy, where the nations hear these laws and say, "Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people."
How could they say that, he asks, if the laws made no sense? Second, his limit.

teach.h: REASONS FOR THE WHOLE, NOT EACH DETAIL.
teach.b: The general purpose of each commandment has a reason, but not every detail. Why a lamb in one offering and a ram in another? Some choice had to be made, he says, and searching for a reason there is chasing nothing.

teach.h: A STATUTE: KEPT AS A DECREE.
teach.b: The Torah calls the red heifer ritual "the statute of the law," using the word chok, statute. Rashi explains it as a decree: God has decreed it, and a person has no right to question it.
In the Talmud, the rabbis even suggest the reasons were left unrevealed for a purpose, warning that King Solomon, who thought he knew the reasons for the king's laws, stumbled.
Fourth, what both sides share. Neither says to keep only the laws you understand.
For Maimonides, the search for reasons deepens the keeping. For the other view, keeping without knowing is its own kind of trust.

how: Jewish study of a commandment often asks both what the law requires and what its purpose might be. Some teachers draw on Maimonides' reasons; others, following Rashi on the red heifer, stress keeping the statutes as decrees.

o: the fines a court charges for breaking a law
the flavors of the foods eaten at a Passover seder
the search for each commandment's purpose and sense

games.q: you're Maimonides. some people say a law with no explanation is more divine. how do you answer?
o: they're right; reasons diminish the law.
they have it backward; the nations call these laws wise.
laws don't need to be kept anyway.
games.why: he points to Deuteronomy: the nations will say, 'surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.' that needs laws that make sense.

practice: Choose one practice you know, from Judaism or your own life, lighting candles, resting one day a week, no phones at dinner, and ask Maimonides' question: what is this for, what idea does it teach, what habit does it shape?
Then ask the other question: is there something here I keep even without a full answer? Let both answers be there.

wordCard.voice: Ta'amei hamitzvot. The reasons for the commandments: the search Maimonides champions, held alongside the view that some laws are decrees whose reasons we can't know. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the reasons (literally, tastes) of the commandments.

carryVoice: Your line: looking for reasons. A rule can be kept with a why, or kept in trust. That's one thousand one hundred fifty-nine days.
